chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal and his son, said:

They wrote to the Man (peace be upon him): 'May God be our ransom for you. We are a people who make swords, and we have no livelihood or trade other than this, and we are compelled to do so. Our treatment (for ritual purity) is from the skins of the domestic donkeys and mules (which are not slaughtered), and no other [skin] is permissible in our work. Therefore, is it permissible for us to work with them, buy them, sell them, and touch them with our hands and clothes, while we pray in our clothes? We are in need of your answer to this matter, O our Master, due to our necessity for it.'

He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'Make a separate garment for prayer.' And I wrote to him: 'May God be my ransom. I take the sword hilts, which are called safan, from fish skins. Is it permissible for me to work with them, since we do not eat their meat?' He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.الْمَيْتَةِ: Animals that died without ritual slaughter (non-halal slaughter)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the ritual purity of skins from non-slaughtered animals for craftsmen?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the practical application of *al-ijaz* (permission) for artisans dependent on specific trades, specifically sword-makers using skins of non-slaughtered equines. While the Imam instructs them to designate a separate garment for prayer to maintain ritual purity, he permits sword hilts made from fish skins, reflecting the Shia juristic consensus that fish skin is inherently pure (*tahir*) regardless of consumption. This ruling highlights the flexibility of fiqh in accommodating economic necessity (*darurah*) without compromising core ritual requirements.
